subject: combined-science

items.q: In physics, what is meant by a system?
items.correct: An object, or a group of objects, being studied.
items.misconception: A machine that has been built to move energy.
items.why: In everyday speech 'system' is used for heating systems, sound systems and computer systems, all of which are manufactured devices. In physics the word is deliberately far wider. The specification defines it in one line: a system is an object or group of objects. You choose the system, and nothing needs to have been built for it to count.
items.random_wrong: A group of two or more objects, never one.

items.q: What always happens when a system changes?
items.correct: The way energy is stored in the system changes.
items.misconception: Some of the energy in the system is used up.
items.why: Everyday language is full of 'using energy', 'energy loss' and 'running out of energy', all of which suggest the energy has gone. Describe every change as stores emptying and other stores filling. 'Used up' usually means 'now in a thermal store of the surroundings, spread out too thinly to be useful'.
items.random_wrong: The amount of energy in the system rises.

items.q: Which of these is a way of storing energy rather than a way of transferring it?
items.correct: The elastic store of a squashed spring.
items.misconception: The heating of a large beaker of cold water.
items.why: Older courses taught 'heat energy', 'electrical energy' and 'sound energy' as types of energy, and the habit of listing them as stores survives. Keep the two lists apart. Stores: kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic, nuclear. Transfers: heating, work done by forces, work done when a current flows, and by waves.
items.random_wrong: The work done by a steady pushing force.

items.q: The specification asks for all the changes in the way energy is stored when a system changes. What must such a description name?
items.correct: Each store that empties and each that fills.
items.misconception: Only the useful store that fills in the change.
items.why: Diagrams in advertising and in some textbooks show only the useful output, and the dissipated energy is left off because it is not wanted. Draw every bar, including the thermal store of the surroundings. The diagram is a way of showing that the total is redistributed, and it only works if nothing is left out.
items.random_wrong: Only the store that empties during the change.

items.q: A ball is thrown straight upwards. As it rises, what happens to the way energy is stored?
items.correct: The kinetic store empties and the gravitational store fills.
items.misconception: The gravitational store empties, the kinetic store fills.
items.why: 'Moving' is linked to 'kinetic', so any motion is taken to mean the kinetic store is filling, regardless of whether the object is speeding up or slowing down. The kinetic store depends on speed, not on movement as such. A ball thrown upwards slows down as it rises, so its kinetic store empties as its gravitational store fills.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic store keeps filling while the ball rises.

items.q: Air resistance is ignored. At the highest point of a ball's flight, what has happened to the energy that was in its kinetic store?
items.correct: It has all been transferred to the gravitational store.
items.misconception: It was destroyed at the moment the ball stopped.
items.why: Everyday language is full of 'using energy', 'energy loss' and 'running out of energy', all of which suggest the energy has gone. Describe every change as stores emptying and other stores filling. 'Used up' usually means 'now in a thermal store of the surroundings, spread out too thinly to be useful'.
items.random_wrong: It has been transferred to the elastic store of the air.

items.q: A trolley moving along a bench hits a wall and stops. What happens to the energy in its kinetic store?
items.correct: It is transferred to thermal stores and by sound.
items.misconception: It is destroyed by the impact of the trolley on the wall.
items.why: The energy becomes invisible: the trolley stops, nothing obvious moves, and a very small temperature rise cannot be felt. Look for where the energy has gone rather than assuming it has gone. Warm, dented metal and a loud bang are the evidence that the energy has been spread into thermal stores and waves.
items.random_wrong: It is used up in bringing the trolley to a stop.

items.q: A constant horizontal force pushes a box along a smooth, level floor. Which store fills as the box speeds up?
items.correct: The kinetic store of the moving box.
items.misconception: The chemical store of the pushing force.
items.why: Force and energy are both introduced as things that make objects move, and 'the force runs out' is a natural way to explain why an object eventually stops. A force is an interaction, not something an object holds. When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done and energy moves between stores; the object holds energy, never force.
items.random_wrong: The gravitational store of the moving box.

items.q: A car slows down when the driver brakes. Which statement describes the changes in the way energy is stored?
items.correct: The kinetic store empties and the thermal stores of the brakes fill.
items.misconception: The kinetic store empties into the chemical store of the brakes.
items.why: Students know the brakes are where the change happens and reach for the chemical store because it is the one they associate with cars and fuel. Chemical stores empty in reactions such as burning; friction does not fill them. Friction between brake pad and disc does work that fills thermal stores, which is why brakes get hot.
items.random_wrong: Energy is lost from the car, so the total energy falls.

items.q: A cyclist stops pedalling on level ground and slowly freewheels to a stop. Which store empties?
items.correct: The kinetic store of the cyclist and the bicycle.
items.misconception: The chemical store held in the cyclist's leg muscles.
items.why: Students learn to label diagrams with stores and feel that every object in the picture needs one, so a store is attached to the nearest available object. Ask what would have to be true for that store to change: has the object moved faster, been raised, been stretched, or become warmer? If the answer is no, the store is not part of the description.
items.random_wrong: The gravitational store of the moving bicycle.

items.q: Water is brought to the boil in an electric kettle. Which statement describes the main change in the way energy is stored?
items.correct: The current does work and the water's thermal store fills.
items.misconception: The chemical store of the kettle itself empties into the water.
items.why: The chemical store is the one most often met as a source, and a kettle is a self-contained object that looks as though it must hold something. A kettle stores nothing until it is plugged in. The energy arrives from the mains while the current flows, which is why unplugging the kettle stops the heating at once.
items.random_wrong: The water gains a store of electrical energy as it is heated.

items.q: As well as the water, which other thermal stores fill while a kettle boils?
items.correct: Those of the kettle and of the air around it.
items.misconception: Only the water's store; nothing else becomes warm.
items.why: Diagrams in advertising and in some textbooks show only the useful output, and the dissipated energy is left off because it is not wanted. Draw every bar, including the thermal store of the surroundings. The diagram is a way of showing that the total is redistributed, and it only works if nothing is left out.
items.random_wrong: None, because the water uses up all the energy.

items.q: 0.50 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 90 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. Using ΔE = m c Δθ, what is the change in thermal energy?
items.why: 4.2 is the value in J/g °C, and it also appears as 4.2 kJ/kg °C, so the digits look familiar while the unit is skipped over. Always substitute the value with the unit that matches the other quantities. With mass in kg and the answer wanted in J, the specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C.

items.q: A heater is switched on under a beaker of water. What does heating the water do?
items.correct: It transfers energy to the water's thermal store.
items.misconception: It raises its temperature but transfers no energy.
items.why: Temperature is the quantity that is measured and talked about, so it takes the place of energy in students' descriptions of heating. Heating is an energy transfer, and a rise in temperature is the evidence that the thermal store has filled. Two objects at the same temperature can hold very different amounts of energy.
items.random_wrong: It fills the kinetic store of the beaker.

items.q: A constant force of 40 N pushes a crate 2.5 m across a floor, in the direction of the force. Using W = F s, how much work is done?
items.why: Most equations met just before this one, such as speed and density, are divisions, so division becomes the default action on a pair of numbers, and a weak candidate who cannot recall the operation adds them instead. Read the equation as it is written: F s means F multiplied by s. A larger force over a longer distance must do more work, so dividing cannot be right.

items.q: A constant resultant force does work on an object moving horizontally along the line of the force. What does this work do?
items.correct: It fills the kinetic store of the object.
items.misconception: It is stored as force inside the moving object.
items.why: Force and energy are both introduced as things that make objects move, and 'the force runs out' is a natural way to explain why an object eventually stops. A force is an interaction, not something an object holds. When a force moves an object through a distance, work is done and energy moves between stores; the object holds energy, never force.
items.random_wrong: It uses up the energy the object already has.

items.q: A 2000 W kettle is switched on for 90 s. Using P = E / t, how much energy is transferred by the current?
items.why: Both are quoted in questions about appliances, and P = E / t contains a division, so a division is carried out on whichever numbers are given. Power is energy transferred each second, so running for longer must transfer more energy. Multiply the power by the time in seconds.

items.q: A current flows through the heating element of a hairdryer. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The current does work, filling the element's thermal store.
items.misconception: The element holds a store of electrical energy inside itself.
items.why: 'Electrical energy' was taught for years as a type of energy, and it is still used loosely in everyday writing about appliances. Electricity is a transfer route, not a store. While the current flows, work is done; the store that fills is the thermal store of the element and then of whatever it heats.
items.random_wrong: The current is used up as it passes through the element.

items.q: An energy diagram drawn to a common scale shows the stores in a system before and after a change. What must be true of the bars?
items.correct: The bars after the change add to the same total.
items.misconception: The total after the change must be smaller than before.
items.why: The word 'lost' is used in class for wasted energy, and a warm road is much harder to picture than a moving car. On a common scale diagram the bars after a change always add up to the same total as before. Dissipation changes where the energy is, never how much there is.
items.random_wrong: Every bar after the change matches a bar before it.

items.q: A lamp is supplied with 500 J of energy. It transfers 60 J to the surroundings by light. Drawn on a common scale, what must the remaining bar show?
items.correct: 440 J, going to thermal stores.
items.misconception: 560 J, the two amounts added together.
items.why: Most equations met just before this one, such as speed and density, are divisions, so division becomes the default action on a pair of numbers, and a weak candidate who cannot recall the operation adds them instead. Read the equation as it is written: F s means F multiplied by s. A larger force over a longer distance must do more work, so dividing cannot be right.
items.random_wrong: 60 J, the same as the light output.

items.q: Can a single object be a system on its own?
items.correct: Yes. The definition is 'an object or group of objects', so one object alone is a perfectly good system.
items.misconception: A system must contain at least two objects interacting with each other.
items.why: The word 'group' is the part students remember, and diagrams in lessons usually show two or more objects together. Read the definition in full. Either half satisfies it: a single falling ball is a system, and so is the ball together with the Earth. Which you choose depends on what you want to describe.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At the top of its flight, does a thrown ball still have energy in its kinetic store?
items.correct: If it was thrown straight up, no: at the highest point it is momentarily still, so the kinetic store is empty.
items.misconception: The ball must still hold some energy in its kinetic store, or it could not come back down.
items.why: It feels as though the ball needs 'movement energy' in reserve to start moving again, and students confuse being at rest with having no energy at all. It comes back down because its gravitational store is now full and the weight still acts. The gravitational store empties again on the way down, refilling the kinetic store.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In ΔE = m c Δθ, which temperature goes into the equation?
items.correct: The temperature change Δθ, that is the final temperature minus the starting temperature.
items.misconception: The final temperature reading, or sometimes the starting one, is substituted instead of the change.
items.why: Δθ is written as a single symbol, and the question usually quotes two temperatures, so one of them is picked up unchanged. The Greek letter delta always means 'change in'. Subtract first, then substitute: water taken from 20 °C to 90 °C has Δθ = 70 °C, not 90 °C and not 20 °C.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In P = E / t, what unit must the time be in?
items.correct: Seconds, so that the power in watts gives the energy in joules.
items.misconception: The time is substituted in minutes or hours without being converted to seconds.
items.why: Everyday times are quoted in minutes, and the equation itself contains no reminder that t must be in seconds. Convert first, then substitute. 90 s stays as 90; 1.5 minutes must become 90 s before it is used.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
